AUDITOR GENERAL'S OFFICE, November 24, 1924.

SIR, - Among the amounts deposited by your department to the credit of Casual Revenue during the fiscal year 1923 -
24 I find an amount of $1, deposited on June 7th, 1923, as having been received from the Commandant of the Royal
Military College, Kingston, on account of the purchase price of the yacht Roamer.

This boat was, I find, purchased by your department during the fiscal year 1918 - 19, for the use of Inspector
C.C. Parker, at the cost of $3,000.

As there is such a striking difference between the original cost of the boat and the merely nominal sum for which it
was transferred to, the Royal Military College, I have to ask for the full particulars connected with the use of this boat
and with its transfer to the Military authorities. I have also to ask if any special authority was obtained for the transfer.


I am, sir, your obedient servant,
WM. KEARNS, Asst. A.G.


The Deputy Superintendent General of Indian Affairs.


DEPARTMENT OF INDIAN AFFAIRS, November 26, 1924.

<!-- page 580 -->
SIR, - In reply to your letter of the 24th instant respecting the yacht Roamer, I have to say that it was transferred to the
Dominion Parks Branch of the Department of the Interior in October, 1920, and that Department transferred it, through
the Purchasing Commission of Canada, to the Royal Military College, Kingston. On the 26th June, 1923, the Dominion
Parks Branch of the Department of the Interior wrote this Department as follows: -



=== EXTRACT FROM HERE (pages 581-584) ===
<!-- page 581 -->
"Enclosed herewith is draft for $1 from Kingston deposited by the Commandant of the Royal Military College to cover
the purchase of the Roamer.

"Although this boat was not secured directly from you by the Royal Military College. this transfer is being put through
in order that the requirements of the Department of Marine and Fisheries may be more readily met than by having a
transfer from your Department to this Department and from this Department to the Royal Military College. (Sgd.)
J.B. Harkin, Commissioner."


Your obedient servant,
J.D. MCLEAN, Asst. Deputy and Sec'y.

Greater Production Account: Payment to H. S. Watwood for Share of Crop and Threshing expenses, Blackfoot
Reserve


AUDITOR GENERAL'S OFFICE, October 6, 1924.

SIR, - Cheque No. 23995, issued by Mr. W.M. Graham, Commissioner at Regina, and charged against his Greater
Production account, is for a payment of $579.10 to H.S. Watwood "for share of crop and amount due for threshing".
The only information I have in connection with this payment is Mr. Watwood's receipt as above.

One of the Greater Production farms on the Blackfoot reserve appears to have been rented to Mr. Watwood on a crop
lease basis. I should like to have full particulars with regard to the agreement entered into with Mr. Watwood as
regards the sowing, harvesting, threshing and marketing the crop. Full particulars of this payment should be furnished
me showing what. part of it was for Watwood's share of the crop, and what part was for Mr. Graham's share of the cost
of the threshing. A detailed statement should also be furnished by Mr. Watwood of the cost of the threshing.


I am, Sir, your obedient servant,
WM. KEARNS, Asst. A.G.


The Deputy Superintendent General of Indian Affairs.


DEPARTMENT OF INDIAN AFFAIRS, October 27, 1924.

SIR, - With reference to letter of the 6th instant, in, which particulars were requested regarding operations carried on
by Mr. H.S. Watwood, on one of the Greater Production Farms on the Blackfoot Reserve, I beg to transmit for your
information copy of a report made in the matter by Mr. W.M. Graham, Indian Commissioner, Regina. The statement
referred to by Mr. Graham is transmitted also. I trust that you will find the information furnished satisfactory.


Your obedient servant,
J.D. MCLEAN, Asst. Deputy and Sec'y.


The Assistant Auditor General.


DEPARTMENT OF INDIAN AFFAIRS, REGINA, October 16, 1924.

SIR, - I am in receipt of your letter of October 8, No. 427,063-104B, in connection with a letter which you received
from the Assistant Auditor General respecting the payment of $579.10 made to Mr. H.S. Watwood for a share of crop

<!-- page 582 -->
on the Blackfoot Reserve.

<!-- page 583 -->
I wish to inform you that Mr. Watwood was our foreman at the Greater Production Farm on the Blackfoot Reserve in
1922, and during that summer a section of land was summer followed by our outfits. In, the fall of that year the Greater
Production Farm at this point was shut down, and the stubble land was all loosed. Mr. Watwood was given a lease on
the section that was summer-followed, and as we had been put to a great deal of expense summer-following this land
during the summer, it was only right that we should receive something in return for this work. The arrangement was
that he was to supply one-half of the seed and we were to supply the other half. We were to receive fifty per cent of
the crop as our share, and as he owned his own threshing machine we were to pay him seven cents per bushel for our
share of the crop. These arrangements were made in this office, and covered the season of 1923.

During the summer of 1923, the crop was very badly hailed and in July it looked as if it was going to be a total failure.
There were, however, a few patches that we cut with a binder, and threshed, and the total proceeds amounted to
1,493 bushels and 30 pounds. This grain was sold to the Alberta Pacific Grain Company, and the total amount received
from them was $1,054.82, which sum was banded to our Agent, Mr. Gooderham, forwarded by him to this office and
credited through the cash book in the regular way.

Mr. Watwood was entitled to $527.41 or 50 per cent, of the $1,054.82. He was also entitled to seven cents per bushel
for threshing our half of the grain, and was paid according to what his machine registered, which was 1,477 bushels.
Our half of that amount was 738 1/2 bushels at 7 cents amounting to $51.69.

I note what the Assistant Auditor General says that a detailed statement should also be furnished by Mr. Watwood as
to the cost of threshing. It would be impossible for Mr. Watwood to give any further statement than the enclosed. The
cost of threshing runs anywhere from 12 cents to 20 cents per bushel, which is ae going price all over western Canada.
You will see that this was a special arrangement that be was to thresh the grain for 7 cents a bushel, which is much
lower than the prevailing price of threshing in the West.

I am herewith attaching a statement and I trust you will find it in order, and that it will be satisfactory to the Asst.
Auditor General.


Your obedient servant,
W.M. GRAHAM, Indian Commr.


The Secretary, Department of Indian Affairs, Ottawa.

Regina Warehouse Account: Parliamentary Authority required for its Continuance


AUDITOR GENERAL'S OFFICE, April 30, 1924.

SIR, - I am in receipt of a copy of an Order in Council of March 7, 1924 (P.C. 33/378) setting forth that Mr.
W.M. Graham, Indian Commissioner at Regina, had on deposit, on December 31, 1923, the amount of $21,700, being
the proceeds arising from the sale of miscellaneous clothing and other merchandise transferred from the Department of
National Defence and from the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment.

This Order provides that, when the amount has been deposited to the credit of the Receiver General, an equal amount
shall be inserted in the estimates as a grant to be expended in the interests of the Indians as the Governor in Council
may from time to time approve.

It has already been pointed out to you in our letter of December 4, 1922, that the procedure followed in disposing of
these stores was not in accordance with the provisions of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, which requires

<!-- page 584 -->
that all public moneys be deposited to the credit of the Receiver General. There is no authority that I can find for the
creation of a special fund of this nature.

The depositing of the balance on hand on December 31, does not legalize the course that has been followed in the past,
nor does it close this Account. A large quantity of goods are still on hand in the Warehouse at Regina, and returns
received from Mr. Graham for the first three months of the present calendar year show that goods are still being
received and being sold by Mr. Graham.

If it is your desire that the disposal of these stores be conducted in the future in the same manner as in the past, special
parliamentary authority so to do should be obtained at the present session of parliament. Otherwise the account should
be closed forthwith, all moneys on hand should be deposited to the credit of the Receiver General and all goods on
hand be transferred to the Chief Salvage Officer to be disposed of by him.


I am, Sir, your obedient servant,
WM. KEARNS, Asst. A.G.


The Deputy Superintendent General of Indian Affairs.


DEPARTMENT OF INDIAN AFFAIRS, June 7, 1924.

DEAR SIR, - I have to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 30th April with reference to the Warehouse
Account of the Indian Commissioner at Regina.

As you are aware, $21,700 has been deposited to the credit of the Receiver General. No special fund can be created
without the authority of Parliament, and this has not yet been obtained. I will draw my Minister's attention to the
closing paragraph of your letter, which refers to the necessity for special parliamentary authority in this regard.


Yours very truly,
D.C. SCOTT, DS.G.


The Assistant Auditor General.

Regina Warehouse Account: Inquiry as to Stock-taking


AUDITOR GENERAL'S OFFICE, June 26, 1924.

SIR, - In the report submitted to me by Mr. J.W. Reid of this office on his examination during the summer of 1923,
into Mr. W.M. Graham's Warehouse Account, he states as follows: -

"I learned that no regular stock-taking had been made since February, 1921, and as since that date a large quantity of
goods has been received at and issued from the Warehouse, there are likely to be considerable discrepancies, although
I would judge the warehouse man to be competent and trustworthy man. I recommended to Mr. Graham that complete
stock-taking be made as soon as possible, by responsible officers, that all worthless articles be destroyed by them and
written off, and that the stock books be adjusted to the result of such stock-taking; and that, after the actual stock on
hand has thus been established, test audits of the stock-in-hand be made at frequent intervals by checking each time a
number of items taken at random."
